report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Stroke risk is assessed using factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking and atrial fibrillation.
However, these factors describe sources of risk but do not reveal how long-term vascular, metabolic and cardiac stress has affected the brain.
Structural MRI can show accumulated brain injury, whereas functional MRI reflects dynamic brain states and may provide complementary information about vulnerability.
Their temporal sequence and predictive value require longitudinal validation.

This Review evaluates brain imaging features as candidate stroke-risk markers and proposes the central autonomic network as a mechanistic framework linking brain function with cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, inflammation and metabolism.
Overview of structural and functional brain-imaging markers relevant to ischemic stroke risk and the proposed CAN framework for stroke vulnerability.

Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, with approximately 7.8 million new cases in 2021. 1 Current prevention and risk stratification largely rely on established vascular and cardiac risk factors, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking, dyslipidaemia and atrial fibrillation, [2] [3] together with clinical risk models derived from these factors. [4] [5] [6] However, these measures primarily capture an individual's risk exposure and do not directly reflect the cumulative effects of long-term vascular, metabolic and cardiac stress on the brain.

text.text: The brain itself may therefore contain information about stroke susceptibility that is not captured by conventional clinical measures.
Brain MRI provides a window into these risk-related cerebral phenotypes.

Structural MRI markers, including cerebral small-vessel-disease burden, brain atrophy and white-matter microstructural injury, reflect accumulated brain damage, and several have been associated with subsequent stroke in longitudinal studies. [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] By contrast, functional MRI can characterize more dynamic aspects of brain function, including spontaneous activity, functional connectivity, network organization and neurovascular coupling.

text.text: However, existing functional imaging studies have largely focused on populations with elevated or related stroke risk, and the reported abnormalities vary substantially in anatomical distribution, network involvement and direction of effects.

No stable, specific and reproducible functional imaging phenotype of stroke risk has yet emerged, and direct prospective validation against first-ever incident stroke remains lacking. [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] Given this heterogeneity, the challenge is not only to identify reproducible regional abnormalities, but also to determine whether these functional alterations can be interpreted within a physiologically grounded and prospectively testable mechanistic framework.

text.text: The central autonomic network (CAN) is one such candidate framework because it participates in the regulation of cardiac rhythm and heart rate, blood pressure, inflammation and metabolic homeostasis, all of which are closely related to stroke susceptibility. [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22] This Review summarizes structural MRI markers supported by longitudinal stroke-outcome data, then evaluates functional MRI phenotypes observed in stroke-risk states, and finally examines whether the CAN can serve as a mechanistically driven candidate framework for understanding the relationship between these functional alterations and stroke-related physiological processes, while generating testable hypotheses for prospective stroke-risk research.

text.text: We conducted a structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science from database inception through July 2026 to identify studies examining brain imaging in relation to ischemic stroke risk, supplemented by screening the reference lists for relevant articles.

Eligible studies primarily examined structural or functional brain imaging in relation to stroke risk or stroke-related high-risk conditions, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, and cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD).

For structural imaging, priority was given to prospective and longitudinal studies with stroke outcomes; for functional imaging and CAN-related evidence, key clinical, physiological, and mechanistic studies were also included.

Structural MRI characterizes brain tissue integrity and the burden of cerebral small vessel disease and currently represents the most mature component of brain-imaging research on stroke prediction. 7, 11, [23] [24] Relevant markers can be grouped into total brain volume, imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease, and white matter microstructural integrity (Table 1).

text.text: These measures primarily reflect the cumulative effects of previous or ongoing vascular risk exposure within the brain and may, to some extent, index the brain reserve available to withstand subsequent ischemic injury.

The assessment of total brain volume (TBV), which combines gray and white matter, is commonly used as a global structural marker of brain integrity. 25 Reduced TBV is widely regarded as an imaging marker of brain atrophy and may reflect the cumulative effects of chronic ischemia and vascular injury. 26 Lower TBV is associated with cSVD, 26 and may also reflect the cumulative impact of vascular risk factors, such as chronic hypertension 27 and inflammation. 28 Earlier studies reported that individuals with higher vascular risk scores had smaller TBV. 29 In the Framingham Heart Study, each standard deviation decrease in total cerebral brain volume (TCBV) was associated with a 51% higher risk of incident stroke (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.13-2.01). 7 This suggests that brain atrophy may reflect a cumulative burden of vascular injury and may serve as a proxy for overall brain health and resilience.

text.text: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are areas of increased signal intensity in the white matter on T2-weighted or FLAIR MRI and are commonly regarded as imaging markers of cSVD. 24 Pathologically, they are thought to reflect chronic ischemic injury and may also involve demyelination and blood-brain barrier disruption. [30] [31] Prospective studies consistently show that WMH burden is associated with both incident and recurrent ischemic stroke. 8, 32 In the Cardiovascular Health Study, annual stroke incidence was 2.8% in individuals with severe WMH versus 0.6% in those with minimal WMH. 8 Similarly, in a large cohort of 7,101 patients with ischemic stroke, higher WMH volume quartiles were associated with a stepwise increase in 1-year risk of recurrent ischemic stroke (HR 1.03, 1.37, and 1.61 across quartiles vs. the lowest). 32 Notably, WMH characteristics beyond total burden may also be clinically relevant.

text.text: In the SMART-MR Study, WMH volume, type, and shape were associated with long-term risk of mortality and ischemic stroke. 33 Together, these findings indicate that WMH burden and morphology capture clinically relevant aspects of cSVD-related brain injury and may contribute to stroke risk stratification.

text.text: Cerebral microbleeds (CMB) are small, round or ovoid hypointense lesions seen on T2*weighted or susceptibility-weighted MRI and are generally regarded as imaging markers of cSVD. 24 They are thought to reflect hemosiderin deposition after prior microscopic bleeding. 34 In the population-based Rotterdam Study, cerebral microbleeds were associated with an increased risk of stroke overall, whereas microbleeds at non-Cerebral-Amyloid-Angiopathy (CAA)-related locations were associated with ischemic stroke. 9 This distinction is critical: CMB in deep or infratentorial regions (e.g., basal ganglia, brainstem) are more likely to reflect hypertensive arteriopathy, while lobar CMB are more often linked to CAA. 34 A higher CMB burden was associated with greater stroke risk, supporting a dose-response relationship between microvascular injury and future cerebrovascular events. 35 This suggests that CMB may reflect microvascular fragility and a heightened risk of both hemorrhagic and ischemic events, possibly due to impaired vascular autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction.

text.text: Lacunes are round or ovoid, fluid-filled cavities measuring 3-15 mm in diameter in the deep gray or white matter, brainstem, or pons, and are generally regarded as neuroimaging markers of cSVD. 24 They are thought to represent the chronic stage of a prior small subcortical infarct or, less commonly, a small hemorrhage.

text.text: Evidence suggests that a greater lacune burden, particularly the presence of multiple lacunes, is associated with an increased risk of recurrent ischemic stroke. 10 In a Danish cohort of 786 patients, single silent lacunes were associated with a numerically higher but non-significant risk of recurrence (HR 1.53, 95% CI 0.67-3.49), whereas multiple lacunes were associated with a significantly higher risk of recurrent ischemic stroke (HR 2.52, 95% CI 1.25-5.09). 10 This dose-response relationship underscores the cumulative impact of small vessel injury on stroke vulnerability.

text.text: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is widely used to characterize white matter microstructural integrity. 36 Commonly derived measures include fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), radial diffusivity (RD), axial diffusivity (AD), 37 and the more recent peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD). [38] [39] These indices are sensitive to subtle abnormalities in normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) 40 and are thought to reflect alterations related to myelin and axonal integrity as well as white matter organization. 41 Because DTI can detect microstructural injury before macroscopic WMH becomes visible, it may serve as a sensitive early marker of cSVD. 38, 40 Evidence from large population-based cohorts, notably the Rotterdam Study, has shown that lower FA and higher MD within NAWM are associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke, independent of age, blood pressure, WMH volume, and other vascular risk factors. 11 Recent genetic evidence further supports the relevance of white matter microstructural pathways to ischemic stroke risk.

Structural MRI markers have a relatively substantial longitudinal evidence base: white matter hyperintensities, greater lacune burden, cerebral microbleeds, and white matter microstructural abnormalities have all been associated with subsequent cerebrovascular events. [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] Overall, these measures have relatively good measurement stability and clinical accessibility, and imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease have relatively wellestablished definitions and reporting standards. 24 Their main limitations are that most reflect tissue injury that has already occurred and have limited etiological specificity.

text.text: Future research should move beyond repeatedly establishing associations with stroke and determine whether individual or combined structural markers provide independent, stable, and clinically actionable incremental value beyond traditional risk models.

Whereas structural MRI reflects cumulative tissue injury, functional MRI (fMRI) characterizes dynamic aspects of brain function -local spontaneous activity, functional connectivity and network organization, and neurovascular coupling -and thus may capture information not evident structurally.
To date, however, no study has acquired functional MRI (fMRI) in stroke-free individuals and shown that it predicts first-ever incident stroke.

The available evidence comes almost entirely from cross-sectional comparisons in populations with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD), or from associations with blood pressure, structural injury, or cognition rather than stroke. [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [44] [45] [46] [47] [48] [49] [50] [51] [52] Three features recur across this literature and should be kept in mind throughout: findings are anatomically heterogeneous and directionally inconsistent; the measures are derived from the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal and are therefore sensitive to cerebral hemodynamics and systemic physiology as well as to neural activity; [53] [54] and reproducibility is constrained by limited test-retest reliability and by analytic choices such as parcellation, motion correction, and physiological-noise removal. [54] [55] [56] [57] These constraints, more than any single regional finding, explain why no reproducible functional phenotype of stroke risk has yet emerged.

text.text: Whether connectivity or topology predicts incident stroke beyond clinical risk factors and structural MRI is therefore untested.

Neurovascular coupling indexes the matching of neural activity to local blood-flow supply, estimated in humans from task-evoked responses or from resting-state cerebral blood flow (CBF)-ALFF, CBF-ReHo, or CBF-connectivity coupling, [77] [78] and is mechanistically closer to vascular vulnerability than isolated activity or connectivity measures.

text.text: Taken together, systemic vascular risk gives rise to functional brain phenotypes that fMRI can detect, but the evidence is cross-sectional and associational and does not show that any measure identifies which individuals will later have a stroke.

Establishing predictive value would require functional MRI acquired in stroke-free individuals at baseline, first-ever stroke as the prospective outcome, adequate within-individual stability, and demonstrable incremental value beyond established risk factors and structural MRI.

Until that evidence chain exists, local activity, functional connectivity, and neurovascular coupling should be regarded as candidate phenotypes of brain vulnerability rather than validated predictors of stroke.
Existing functional imaging studies have not identified a stable, specific, and reproducible phenotype of stroke risk.

This may be because stroke susceptibility is not determined by functional abnormalities in a single brain region but reflects the long-term dysregulation of multiple physiological processes -heart rate and cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, inflammation, and metabolism.

The central autonomic network (CAN) participates in the central regulation of all four and links brain function with peripheral physiological activity. [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22] We therefore propose the CAN not as an established stroke-specific signature but as an organizing framework -a way to specify, a priori, which regions to examine and why.

text.text: The subsections below set out the biological plausibility of this proposal: that CAN circuits regulate cardiac autonomic tone, blood pressure, inflammation, and metabolism, each independently linked to stroke.

We stress at the outset that this plausibility is not evidence of prediction, since no study has explicitly related CAN-derived imaging measures to incident stroke, and the links assembled below are associational.
Definitions of the CAN vary across conceptual and neuroimaging frameworks.

Across neuroimaging meta-analyses, the most consistent convergence is observed in the bilateral insula and midcingulate cortex, which are treated here as the imaging-defined core, while the inferior parietal lobule forms part of an extended functional network. [82] [83] Broader conceptual and neuroimaging frameworks additionally include the amygdala, medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices, hypothalamus, hippocampal formation, mediodorsal thalamus, precuneus, cerebellum, periaqueductal gray, parabrachial complex, nucleus tractus solitarius, and ventrolateral medulla.

text.text: Under physiological conditions, the CAN coordinates parasympathetic and sympathetic outflow through interconnected insula, cingulate cortex (ACC), hypothalamus and brainstem circuits, contributing to cardiovascular autonomic regulation and heart-rate variability (HRV). 17, [21] [22] Within this network, the insula is a key cortical region for autonomic cardiovascular control, as shown by insular cortex stimulation studies. 84 Clinically, insular involvement has been associated with reduced HRV and a higher risk of arrhythmias or other adverse cardiac manifestations. 85 Rs-fMRI studies in stroke high-risk populations, particularly in cSVD, have shown alterations in intrinsic networks, including salience-network regions such as the insula and ACC, as well as altered local spontaneous activity reflected by changes in amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo). 16, 68 HRV-fMRI coupling provides a more direct functional readout of autonomic-central interactions. 86 Prospective population-based evidence links peripheral autonomic imbalance -higher resting heart rate and lower heart-rate variability -to incident stroke, 87 establishing that autonomic dysregulation carries stroke risk.

text.text: This peripheral evidence does not, however, show that central, CAN-derived imaging measures predict stroke: it motivates, rather than validates, their prospective evaluation.
Beyond heart rate and rhythm regulation, the CAN is also involved in central blood pressure control.

Early electrical stimulation studies in epilepsy patients showed that insular stimulation could induce bradycardia and depressor responses. 84 A later electrical stimulation study in patients with epilepsy suggested a direct role of the insula in central blood pressure regulation. 88 Rs-fMRI studies further demonstrated that functional connectivity among CAN-related regions, including the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, thalamus, amygdala, and brainstem, was associated with baroreflex sensitivity, supporting a close link between CAN network state and blood pressure regulatory function. 89 Furthermore, in APOE ε4 carriers, lower resting-state CAN functional connectivity strengthened the association between beat-to-beat blood pressure variability and cSVD burden, whereas CAN connectivity did not mediate this relationship. 90 Meanwhile, higher blood pressure variability has been shown to predict subsequent stroke independently of mean blood pressure and to be associated with greater cSVD burden, particularly WMH. 91- 92 Taken together, these observations are consistent with a link between altered CAN functional connectivity, blood-pressure instability, and small-vessel brain injury; whether this constellation carries information about future stroke, beyond blood pressure itself, remains to be tested prospectively.

text.text: The CAN is also involved in the central regulation of inflammation.

Vagus nerve stimulation has been reported to inhibit peripheral inflammatory markers, including TNF, IL-6, and IL-1β. 93 In a previous study, lower HRV was also associated with higher levels of C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, suggesting a link between autonomic regulation and systemic inflammatory burden. 94 At the functional imaging level, higher peripheral IL-6 levels were associated with stronger functional connectivity of the subgenual ACC within the DMN. 95 In addition, a double-blind randomized study showed that acute systemic inflammation induced by low-dose lipopolysaccharide increased resting-state connectivity between the left anterior insula and the left midcingulate cortex. 96 Inflammation is also linked to cSVD, with higher CRP and IL-6 levels being associated with greater WMH burden. 97 Prospective evidence has further shown that higher circulating IL-6 levels are associated with an increased risk of incident ischemic stroke. 98 Collectively, these findings suggest that altered inflammatory regulation may represent one pathway linking CAN-related alterations to cSVD-related WMH and increased stroke susceptibility.

text.text: The CAN-related circuits are also involved in the central regulation of metabolic homeostasis.

For example, in patients with refractory obesity, hypothalamic deep brain stimulation has been reported to acutely increase resting metabolic rate and sleep energy expenditure, suggesting that CAN-related circuits may contribute to energy balance regulation. 99 Meanwhile, in patients with type 2 diabetes, an rs-fMRI study found increased degree centrality in the right anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, suggesting stronger functional connections with other brain regions.

text.text: However, the role of the CAN in stroke susceptibility remains largely inferential, and prospective studies directly linking CAN-related functional alterations to incident stroke are still lacking.
CAN-related functional measures should therefore be regarded as candidate markers requiring prospective validation rather than established predictors of stroke risk.
Before considering how such markers might be validated and translated into clinical practice, it is useful to place them within the broader landscape of imaging biomarkers in neurological disease.
The proposition that brain imaging can index the risk of a systemic vascular event is rare in stroke medicine, but it is not without precedent.

The closest analogy is Alzheimer's disease, where imaging biomarkers have traveled the full distance from descriptive correlates to a biologically defined framework that now guides trial enrollment and therapeutic decisions. [105] [106] That trajectory is instructive in three respects.

text.text: First, biomarkers gained traction only once they were anchored to an explicit mechanistic model rather than accumulated as a list of group differences.

The amyloid-tauneurodegeneration construct succeeded because each marker was assigned a defined position in a hypothesized causal sequence. 107 The CAN framework proposed here is intended to provide a similar organizing framework for stroke: it specifies a priori which regions should be evaluated and why, and it makes falsifiable predictions-that CANrelated functional measures should relate to autonomic, blood pressure, inflammatory, and metabolic phenotypes, and should carry predictive information beyond established clinical risk factors and structural cSVD burden.

text.text: Second, progress depended on methodological harmonization.

Standardized data acquisition, common quantitative scales, and shared multicentre infrastructure converted heterogeneous findings into comparable measurements. 105, 108 Stroke research has achieved something similar for structural small-vessel-disease markers, where consensus reporting standards permit WMH, lacunes, and microbleeds to be compared across cohorts. 24 No equivalent standard exists for resting-state functional measures, representing one major obstacle to translation.

text.text: Third, progress also depended on establishing the temporal ordering of biomarkers.

The corresponding task here is to determine whether CAN functional alterations precede autonomic and hemodynamic instability, which in turn precede accelerating small-vessel injury, or whether the sequence runs in the opposite direction.
Two differences from the neurodegenerative setting shape what success would look like.
Stroke is an acute, partly stochastic event with competing extracerebral causes, not a slowly progressive proteinopathy; and much of its risk is already captured by established clinical instruments.
The benchmark for a brain-based marker is therefore not diagnostic classification but demonstrable incremental value over existing risk scores and established structural imaging markers.

If the framework is supported by future prospective studies, its practical consequence may be that stroke risk assessment could incorporate a measure of central regulatory state alongside conventional vascular and cardiac variables.
Four developments would be required.
Individual markers are unlikely to be sufficient on their own.

A composite CAN-informed phenotype could combine structural burden (WMH volume and shape, lacunes, microbleeds, PSMD), white matter microstructure along CANrelevant pathways, resting-state connectivity within the prespecified cortical CAN node set, and perfusion-based neurovascular coupling.
Non-canonical regions should be analysed separately rather than added post hoc to the core node set.

Because these modalities capture complementary aspects of brain vulnerability, including accumulated damage, current network state, and vascular responsiveness, their combination may be more informative than any single index and could be summarized in a compact form analogous to established brain-age or global-burden scores.
Data-driven imaging signatures.

Machine learning offers a means of deriving such composites empirically rather than by expert weighting, and of detecting spatial patterns that region-of-interest analyses miss. 109 Realizing this will require training on cohorts with prospectively ascertained incident stroke rather than on case-control contrasts, since the latter risk learning the consequences of established disease.

text.text: Given the modest sample sizes typical of functional imaging studies, external validation in independent cohorts, explicit calibration assessment, and interpretability constraints that keep models anatomically accountable are essential; otherwise apparent performance will not survive replication.
Coupling central imaging with continuous peripheral physiology.
Imaging characterizes the central state at a single time point, whereas the pathophysiology proposed here is dynamic.

Heart rate variability, baroreflex sensitivity, and beat-to-beat blood pressure variability provide the corresponding peripheral readout, and HRV-fMRI coupling already offers a direct index of central-autonomic interaction. 86 Wearable and ambulatory technologies extend this to continuous, real-world monitoring of rhythm and autonomic tone, 110 allowing a static central phenotype to be paired with longitudinal peripheral output.

text.text: This combined central-peripheral autonomic phenotype, rather than imaging alone, may therefore represent a promising strategy for future translational studies.
Incorporation into clinical risk models.

The decisive test is whether such a phenotype improves prediction beyond established instruments and structural MRI markers. [4] [5] [6] This requires evaluation in prospective cohorts using discrimination, calibration, reclassification, and decision-analytic measures, with attention to whether reclassification occurs in individuals for whom management would actually change.

text.text: Finally, the framework implies an intervention-based test that imaging association studies cannot provide: if CAN dysfunction contributes causally to stroke vulnerability, then interventions that modify central autonomic regulation should alter intermediate phenotypes such as blood pressure variability, inflammatory burden, and arrhythmia propensity in a predictable direction.

Such studies would help determine whether CANrelated functional alterations are merely markers of an underlying risk state or mechanistic contributors to its development, moving the CAN from a framework that organizes existing observations to one that generates testable therapeutic hypotheses.
Brain imaging may provide information about stroke susceptibility that is complementary to conventional clinical risk factors.

Structural MRI markers reflect accumulated vascular brain injury and are supported by a relatively substantial longitudinal evidence base, whereas functional measures, including local activity, functional connectivity, network organization, and neurovascular coupling, capture more dynamic alterations associated with vascular risk and related cerebrovascular conditions.
However, current functional imaging findings remain heterogeneous, and no stable or reproducible functional phenotype of stroke risk has yet been established.

Within this context, the CAN is proposed not as an established stroke-specific imaging signature, but as a mechanistically grounded framework linking central functional states to cardiac autonomic regulation, blood pressure, inflammation, and metabolism.
The key question is therefore whether CAN-related functional measures can provide information beyond conventional vascular and cardiac risk factors and structural MRI markers.

Addressing this question will require prospective studies in stroke-free populations that directly evaluate incident stroke and test the stability, reproducibility, and incremental predictive value of CAN-related measures.
If validated, such measures could contribute to a more integrated assessment of stroke susceptibility.

Central autonomic network dysfunction may contribute to cSVD-related brain injury through four major physiological pathways, including dysregulation of heart rate and cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, inflammation, and metabolism. cSVD-related brain injury may subsequently increase stroke vulnerability.
In parallel, CAN-related functional MRI measures may capture functional brain alterations linked to these pathways and may serve as candidate brain predictors of stroke risk.
